doc.title: Michael Moore interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: Jazz parties as a circuit
summary: Moore likes the jazz parties but dislikes their pickup-jam nature, and credits Joe with mixing in organized groups.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: It’s interesting, even tonight it looks like they have a set-up where the people are going to be eating dinner during the first significant portion of this party. These jazz parties are an interesting kind of phenomenon. Do you enjoy making the circuit on these things?

I do. I’ve been doing them now for I guess I started doing them back in the mid 70s I think. So I’ve been doing them a long time. I actually enjoy some more than others, depending on the circumstances. The thing that I don’t like about them is the fact that they’re big jam sessions, and the lack of organization that goes on, because of the nature of the beast. I mean it’s a phenomenon that in a way has taken the place of a lot of clubs and things of yesteryear that are no longer in existence. And I’m grateful for them, but again, I think it’s sad that everybody’s hired as an individual. It’s like the George Steinbrenner way of running a baseball team. You hire stars. And that doesn’t necessarily mean that they’re going to play well together. You know whereas you could take any one of these guys that you’ve got here and say why don’t you bring your group, or a group of guys, and maybe have four or five different groups, as opposed to a name horn player from California, a name horn player from Australia, and everybody meets and says, “What are we going to play?” So I think that’s the down side of it. At the same time there’s also some magic that happens when you throw those things together too, that may not have happened either. But I think that the thing that I see running through the last twenty years of doing them is this same kind of lack of groups. Now there are a few of the guys that have done it so much that they make you think it was already thought out and well done, almost organized.
Maybe some kind of balance would be nice, if they had a band during part of the evening and then did the more traditional format.
Which I think Joe tries to do here.

He has some groups. And Becky Kilgore and Dave have recorded together so they have material to work from. And then you have somebody like Dave McKenna, which is like a whole orchestra by himself. And so Joe knows how to do it and he knows how to mix guys — like Cal and I doing a duo together, and we have played together over the years. And he knows, to a degree, what’s going to work. And it’s just again, there’s not many groups around anymore, except a few very famous ones.
